title: Engage in sustained oral/signed communication and evaluate spoken/signed texts

lessons.title: Speaking with purpose
lessons.html:
Sustained communication at work

Sustained oral or signed communication means taking part in longer exchanges: leading a team briefing, presenting a report, negotiating with a supplier, explaining a procedure to clients on a trail ride, or taking part in a meeting. At NQF level 4 you must plan what you say, adjust to your audience and evaluate what others say.

Plan your message

  1. Purpose: to inform, instruct, persuade, negotiate or build relationships?
  2. Audience: grooms, the farm owner, clients, children, a vet? What do they already know, which language do they prefer, and what do they need from you?
  3. Structure: introduction (what this is about), body (main points in a logical order), conclusion (summary and next steps).
  4. Supporting material: examples, figures, a demonstration with a horse or piece of tack.

Delivery

  • Speak clearly at a steady pace; pause after key points.
  • Use words your audience understands. Explain technical terms like "laminitis" or "biosecurity".
  • Use the language most people in the group are comfortable with, or arrange interpretation, including sign language interpretation for Deaf colleagues.
  • Make eye contact and use open body language. In sign language, facial expression carries grammar and meaning.
  • Check understanding: ask open questions such as "What will you do if the horse pulls back?"

Adjusting register

Register is the level of formality. A safety briefing to staff can be direct and simple; a presentation to the board or a call with a client needs a more formal tone. Respect cultural norms of greeting and address, such as greeting before business and using titles for elders.

lessons.title: Listening, interacting and evaluating spoken texts
lessons.html:
Active listening

Communication is two-way. Active listening means:

  • Giving full attention: put the phone away, face the speaker.
  • Showing you are listening: nodding, short responses, signing acknowledgement.
  • Asking clarifying questions.
  • Summarising: "So what you are saying is that the mare has not eaten since yesterday evening."
  • Holding back judgement until the person has finished.

Taking part in discussions

  • Take turns; do not interrupt.
  • Build on others' ideas and give reasons for your views.
  • Disagree respectfully: criticise ideas, not people.
  • Help reach a decision by summarising points of agreement.

Evaluating spoken and signed texts

You will hear many spoken texts at work: a sales pitch from a feed rep, a radio report on drought, a vet's explanation, a political speech about land. Evaluate them critically:

AskWhy
What is the speaker's purpose?To inform, sell or persuade?
Is it fact or opinion?Facts can be checked; opinions are views.
What evidence is given?Figures, trials, experience, or none?
Is there bias?Does the speaker gain from your decision?
Which techniques are used?Repetition, emotional language, exaggeration, appeals to authority
What is left out?Costs, risks, other options

For example, a feed rep who claims a supplement "doubles performance" without data is using exaggeration. Ask for trial results and compare costs in rands before deciding.

Key points

  • Plan purpose, audience and structure before speaking.
  • Choose language and register that suit the audience; arrange interpreting when needed.
  • Listen actively and summarise to check understanding.
  • Disagree respectfully and help the group reach decisions.
  • Evaluate spoken texts for purpose, fact versus opinion, evidence and bias.
